mu-e1a14656.stem: Which tendon changes direction around the dorsal tubercle of the radius (Lister's tubercle)?
mu-e1a14656.explanation: In the 3rd compartment the EPL tendon uses Lister's tubercle as a pulley to turn towards the thumb. After distal radius fractures, friction and impaired blood supply at this point can lead to delayed rupture.

mu-e87f10a7.stem: Where do the lumbricals of the hand arise?
options: From the sides of the metacarpals
From the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus
From the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis
mu-e87f10a7.explanation: The lumbricals arise from the deep flexor tendons and attach to the radial border of the extensor expansion; they flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints. The 1st and 2nd lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve, the 3rd and 4th by the ulnar nerve. The interossei arise from the metacarpals.

mu-e0d255b7.stem: Which bony structures bound Guyon's canal (ulnar canal)?
mu-e0d255b7.explanation: Guyon's canal lies between the pisiform (medially) and the hook of the hamate (laterally), between the palmar carpal ligament and the flexor retinaculum; the ulnar nerve and ulnar artery pass through it. Compression is common in cyclists; because the dorsal cutaneous branch does not enter the canal, sensation on the back of the hand is preserved.

mu-7a6bfa60.stem: Which is the principal muscle producing opposition of the thumb?
mu-7a6bfa60.explanation: Opponens pollicis draws the 1st metacarpal forwards and medially and rotates it medially, bringing the pulp of the thumb against the other fingers. It is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve; injury to this branch abolishes opposition.

mu-d90339d8.stem: In a patient with a glass cut on the ulnar border of the hand, only the deep branch of the ulnar nerve is divided. Which of the following findings is NOT expected?
options: Sensory loss over the hypothenar region and little finger
Weakness in gripping paper between the fingers
mu-d90339d8.explanation: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve is purely motor: it supplies the hypothenar muscles, the interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, adductor pollicis and the deep head of FPB. Sensation of the hypothenar skin and little finger is carried by the superficial branch and is therefore preserved.

options: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
Medial lip of the linea aspera
mu-2246f952.explanation: The superficial fibres of gluteus maximus insert into the iliotibial tract, its deep lower fibres into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur. It is a powerful extensor and lateral rotator of the hip; it is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve.
notes: This is the insertion of gluteus minimus.
This is the insertion of gluteus medius.
This is the insertion of the adductors.
This is the insertion of iliopsoas.

mu-b75f7ed9.stem: Which muscle inserts into the anterior surface of the greater trochanter?
mu-b75f7ed9.explanation: Gluteus minimus inserts into the anterior surface of the greater trochanter, medius into its lateral surface and piriformis into its upper border. Obturator externus attaches in the trochanteric fossa and quadratus femoris to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest.

mu-7a258ce2.stem: Which lateral rotator of the hip has a tendon that passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?
mu-7a258ce2.explanation: Obturator internus arises inside the pelvis; as its tendon leaves through the lesser sciatic foramen it turns at a right angle over the lesser sciatic notch and runs between the gemelli to the greater trochanter. Piriformis passes through the greater sciatic foramen; the others lie outside the pelvis.

mu-86c6ad90.stem: A patient who sits for long periods on hard surfaces has pain radiating from the buttock down the back of the leg; it worsens with the hip in flexion, adduction and internal rotation, and lumbar MRI is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mu-86c6ad90.explanation: The sciatic nerve usually passes below piriformis (sometimes through it); stretching or hypertrophy of the muscle can compress the nerve and cause sciatica that does not originate in the spine. The FAIR position (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) stretches the muscle and so increases the pain.

mu-6dbae2eb.stem: Which muscle covers the roof (anteromedial wall) of the adductor canal?
mu-6dbae2eb.explanation: The lateral wall of Hunter's canal is vastus medialis and its posterior wall adductor longus and magnus; the roof is formed by the vasto-adductor membrane with sartorius over it. The femoral artery and vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis pass through the canal.
notes: It forms the posterior wall of the canal.
It is not related to the canal.
It forms the lateral wall of the canal.
It forms the posterior wall of the canal.

options: Into the medial condyle of the femur
Into the head of the fibula
Into the upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
mu-83bc2675.explanation: Gracilis is a long thin muscle on the medial side of the thigh arising from the inferior pubic ramus; with sartorius and semitendinosus it forms the pes anserinus. It adducts the hip and flexes the knee; it is supplied by the obturator nerve.

mu-77614070.stem: What is the main function of the lower oblique fibres of vastus medialis (VMO)?
options: Preventing lateral displacement of the patella
mu-77614070.explanation: The VMO fibres attach to the patella from the medial side at a nearly horizontal angle; by balancing the laterally pulling component of quadriceps they keep the patella in the trochlea. Weakness predisposes to patellofemoral pain and lateral patellar dislocation. The muscle that pulls the bursa upwards is articularis genus.

mu-de9e803e.stem: Which muscles form the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa?
options: Plantaris and the lateral head of gastrocnemius
mu-de9e803e.explanation: The superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa is semimembranosus and semitendinosus, the superolateral boundary biceps femoris, and the inferior boundaries the medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius (plantaris accompanies the lateral head).
notes: They are at the inferolateral boundary.
They do not take part in the boundaries of the fossa.

mu-4a014f0f.stem: What do the hamstring muscles have in common?
options: They arise from the ischial tuberosity and cross both the hip and knee joints
All are supplied by the femoral nerve
The short head of biceps femoris also fully meets these criteria
All insert into the head of the fibula
mu-4a014f0f.explanation: The true hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, the long head of biceps femoris and the hamstring part of adductor magnus) arise from the ischial tuberosity, extend the hip and flex the knee, and are supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve. The short head of biceps femoris arises from the linea aspera, crosses only the knee and is supplied by the fibular part.
